stem: A model has `contract: {enforced: true}` and specifies a `data_type` for every column. A stakeholder asks whether dbt checks the actual row values against those declared types at runtime -- for example, rejecting a row where a column typed `integer` somehow contains a non-numeric string mid-build. What's the accurate answer?

option_texts.A: No; the contract's preflight check verifies the query's returned column names and data types match the declared schema, it does not inspect individual row values for a hidden type mismatch
option_texts.B: Yes; dbt scans every row during the build column by column and rejects any value that doesn't match the declared type
option_texts.C: Yes, but only for numeric columns; string and timestamp column values are never checked against their declared column type
option_texts.D: No; contracts are purely cosmetic documentation and have no bearing on whether the model actually builds

drill_answer_short: A contract's preflight check compares declared column names/types to the query's output shape, not individual row values
decision_hinge: dbt will run a preflight check to ensure that the model's query will return a set of columns with names and data types matching the ones you have defined, or it will fail to build.

plausible_options.C: whether dbt checks the actual row values against those declared types at runtime

eliminated_by.B: whether dbt checks the actual row values against those declared types at runtime

D.requires_fact: dbt will run a preflight check to ensure that the model's query returns columns with names and data types matching the contract, or it will fail to build, so a contract clearly does affect whether the model builds.

distractor_traps.B: T1: fabricated — the documented preflight check compares the query's output shape, it does not scan individual row values
distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — the preflight check applies uniformly to every declared column, not only numeric ones
distractor_traps.D: T4: breaks a stated fact — a contract violation is documented to fail the build, so it is not merely documentation

stem: A model `dim_listings_cleansed` defines `latest_version: 2`, with versions `v: 1` and `v: 2` both declared. A downstream model that was written against the old shape needs to keep building against version 1 specifically, even though version 2 is now the default for an unversioned `ref()`. Which call pins it to version 1?

option_texts.B: `ref('dim_listings_cleansed')`, since any `ref()` without an explicit version resolves to the oldest declared version
option_texts.C: `ref('dim_listings_cleansed_v1')`, treating the version suffix as part of the base model name
option_texts.D: `ref('dim_listings_cleansed', latest_version=1)`, overriding the model's own `latest_version` property per call

drill_answer_short: Pin a version explicitly with ref('model', v=N)
decision_hinge: ref('dim_customers', v=2) resolves to a specific declared version's database relation, independent of which version is marked latest_version on the model itself.

plausible_options.C: needs to keep building against version 1 specifically, even though version 2 is now the default

B.signal: even though version 2 is now the default for an unversioned `ref()`
B.requires_fact: If latest_version is not specified explicitly, it is the numerically greatest version that is latest; an unversioned ref() resolves to latest_version, which here is explicitly 2, not the oldest version.

eliminated_by.D: even though version 2 is now the default for an unversioned `ref()`

distractor_traps.B: T4: breaks a stated fact — the stem says version 2 is the default, which contradicts resolving to the oldest
distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — the underlying file may carry a version suffix, but ref() still takes the base model name plus a version argument
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — ref() has no per-call latest_version override argument

stem: A team adds `not_null`, `foreign_key`, `unique`, and `check` constraints to a contracted model on Postgres. The data governance lead needs to know how many of these four constraint types Postgres actually enforces at build time, not merely records as metadata. How many are enforced?

option_texts.A: All four; on Postgres, not_null, primary_key, foreign_key, unique, and check are all both definable and enforced
option_texts.B: Only `not_null`; the other three are definable but not enforced on any platform, including Postgres
option_texts.C: Only `not_null` and `foreign_key`; `unique` and `check` are never enforced on any relational warehouse
option_texts.D: None of them; Postgres only supports constraints as comments, with zero enforcement at build time

drill_answer_short: On Postgres, not_null, primary_key, foreign_key, unique, and check are all definable and enforced
decision_hinge: On Postgres: not_null is Definable and Enforced. primary_key is Definable and Enforced. foreign_key is Definable and Enforced. unique is Definable and Enforced. check is Definable and Enforced.

plausible_options.B: The data governance lead needs to know how many of these four constraint types Postgres actually enforces at build time

eliminated_by.C: The data governance lead needs to know how many of these four constraint types Postgres actually enforces at build time
eliminated_by.D: The data governance lead needs to know how many of these four constraint types Postgres actually enforces at build time

distractor_traps.B: T3: confusable sibling — that enforcement pattern describes other platforms, like BigQuery, not Postgres
distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — this enforcement pattern describes platforms like Snowflake or BigQuery, not Postgres
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — Postgres genuinely enforces these constraints at build time, it does not treat them as comments only

stem: A team wants to enforce a contract on `dim_customers`, and defines `constraints` on the `customer_id` column, but leaves `data_type` unset on two other columns in the YAML. The team needs to know whether this is a valid enforced contract as written. Is it?

option_texts.A: No; `contract: enforced: true` requires an explicit `data_type` declared for every column in the schema config, not only the ones with a constraint
option_texts.B: Yes; only columns with an explicit constraint need a declared data_type, the rest are inferred automatically
option_texts.C: Yes; `data_type` is optional everywhere as long as at least one column declares a constraint
option_texts.D: No; a contract additionally requires every single column to carry its own constraint, beyond just a data_type

drill_answer_short: An enforced contract requires a declared data_type for every column, regardless of which columns carry constraints
decision_hinge: You enforce a contract: this means you need to explicitly define the data_type for every column in your model's schema configuration.

plausible_options.B: defines `constraints` on the `customer_id` column, but leaves `data_type` unset on two other columns

eliminated_by.C: The team needs to know whether this is a valid enforced contract as written
eliminated_by.D: defines `constraints` on the `customer_id` column, but leaves `data_type` unset on two other columns

distractor_traps.B: T3: confusable sibling — dbt requires a declared type for every column, not only the ones carrying a constraint
distractor_traps.C: T1: fabricated — a single constrained column does not exempt the rest of the model from declaring data_type
distractor_traps.D: T3: confusable sibling — constraints are optional per column; a declared data_type on every column is the actual requirement
